 1                                 I. INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.   My name is Celia B. Hashlamoun. My business address is 111 East Broadway,

 4        Suite 1200, Salt Lake City, Utah, 84111.

 5   Q.   BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED AND IN WHAT CAPACITY?

 6   A.   I am a Senior Consultant in the firm of Energy Strategies, LLC. Energy Strategies

 7        is a private consulting firm specializing in economic and policy analysis applicable

 8        to energy production, transportation, and consumption.

 9   Q.   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

10   A.   My testimony is being sponsored by the New Mexico Large Customer Group

11        (“NMLCG”). NMLCG is an informal coalition of corporations duly authorized to

12        transact business within the State of New Mexico. NMLCG’s members operate

13        facilities within the service territory of Southwestern Public Service Company

14        (“SPS” or the “Company”), from which they purchase electricity and related energy

15        services.

16   Q.   PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE AND

17        QUALIFICATIONS.

18   A.   I earned a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration from the University of

19        Akron in 2007. I joined Energy Strategies in 2025, where my responsibilities

 2        and developing expert testimony to support regulatory proceedings. Prior to joining

 4        d/b/a Enbridge Gas Ohio. In that role, I was responsible for planning and preparing

 5        analyses that supported various regulatory proceedings and internal business

 6        initiatives.

 7                Before my time at Enbridge Gas Ohio, I worked in the Rates and Regulatory

 8        Affairs Department at FirstEnergy Corp, where I supported regulatory filings and

 9        rate-related analysis. Earlier in my career, I was employed at Plante & Moran

10        Corporate Finance as an Investment Banking Analyst.

12   A.   Yes.    I have testified before in SPS’s most recent Certificates of Public

13        Convenience and Necessity (“CCN”) proceeding, Case No. 25-00066-UT and

14        SPS’s application requesting approval of six Long-Term Purchased Power

16        25-00085-UT.

 7   Q.   WHAT      IS   THE    PURPOSE         OF   YOUR     TESTIMONY        IN   THIS

 8        PROCEEDING?

 9   A.   The purpose of my testimony is to address the following topics:

10             (1) SPS’s revenue requirement,

11             (2) SPS’s jurisdictional allocation of shared system costs, including its

12                 request to directly assign Cunningham BESS costs and benefits to New

13                 Mexico retail customers,

14             (3) SPS’s proposed treatment of federal tax benefits,

15             (4) SPS’s request for approval of cost recovery mechanisms for variable

16                 expenses (including approval of a property tax and excess liability

17                 insurance (“ELI”) tracker, and recovery of Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”)

18                 deficiency payments through the Fuel and Purchased Power Cost

19                 Adjustment Clause (“FPPCAC”)), and

 2                 projects.

 3        NMLCG’s recommendations regarding SPS’s cost of capital and depreciation

 4        expense are provided in the direct testimony of Mr. David Garrett. Mr. Justin Bieber

 5        provides NMLCG’s recommendations regarding the class cost of service study,

 6        class revenue allocation, and rate design.

 7   Q.   WHAT        ARE      THE       PRIMARY           RECOMMENDATIONS                   AND

 8        CONCLUSIONS IN YOUR TESTIMONY?

 9   A.   I offer the following primary recommendations and conclusions:

10           (1) SPS’s proposed increase to its revenue requirement should be decreased by

11               $144.1 million, as supported in my direct testimony and the direct

12               testimony of David Garrett,

13           (2) Condition approval of the direct assignment of the Cunningham BESS on

14               the Company’s proposed 12-CP Production (“12-CP PROD”) jurisdictional

15               allocator being modified to account for the direct assignment, and ensure

16               New Mexico customers receive all associated benefits,

17           (3) Modify the ratemaking treatment of the Cunningham BESS investment tax

18               credit (“ITC”) liability in rates to reflect its treatment at the in-service date.

 6                               III. REVENUE REQUIREMENT

13           requirement of $172,300,149 on an annual basis.3 SPS’s requested revenue increase

14           is calculated using a Future Test Year (“FTY”) for the period December 1, 2026,

15           through November 30, 2027.

 1   Q.   DOES YOUR REVENUE REQUIREMENT CALCULATION ACCOUNT

 8   Q.   DO YOU HAVE ANY GENERAL CONCERNS WITH THE PERIOD OF

 9        THE COMPANY’S FTY?

10   A.   Yes.   The FTY incorporates projected plant additions and rate base changes

11        extending 29 months beyond the end of the base period. SPS developed its FTY by

12        beginning with the Base Period of July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025 (“Base

13        Period”), applying normalizations and annualizations to create an Adjusted Base

14        Period (“Adjusted Base Period”), and then using a linkage data period of July 1,

15        2025 through November 30, 2026 (“Linkage Period”) to bridge to the FTY ending

16        November 30, 2027. While this approach may not violate the N.M. Admin. Code,

17        the length of the forecast period increases the uncertainty associated with projected

18        rate base and expense levels included in rates.

 1                        A.       JURISDICTIONAL ALLOCATION FACTORS

 2   Q.         HOW DOES SPS PROPOSE TO ALLOCATE PROJECT COSTS AND

 3              BENEFITS BETWEEN ITS JURISDICTIONS?

 4   A.         As explained by Company Witness Taylor Hurt, SPS uses three main allocation

 5              factors to allocated joint system costs that are not directly assigned:

 6              (1) Line-loss-adjusted kilowatt-hour (“kWh”) energy allocator for production

 7                   energy costs including rate base, O&M, depreciation, taxes, and other costs;

 8              (2) Line-loss-adjusted production-related 12-CP demand allocator for production

 9                   rate base, O&M, depreciation, taxes, and other costs; and

10              (3) a line-loss-adjusted transmission-related 12-CP allocator for transmission

11                   related rate base, O&M, depreciation, taxes, and other costs.5

12       Q.      IS THE COMPANY REQUESTING TO DIRECTLY ALLOCATE ANY

13               SPECIFIC PRODUCTION ASSETS TO THE NEW MEXICO RETAIL

14               JURISDICTION IN THIS CASE?

15   A.         Yes. As stated in the testimony of Ms. Lees, the Company is requesting that all

16              costs associated with Cunningham BESS be assigned to New Mexico retail

17              customers. While the New Mexico Commission approved the CCN associated with

13             ALLOCATION METHODOLOGY?

14   A.        This indicates that the Company’s allocation methodology treats generation

15             resources as shared assets and does not reflect asset-specific assignments. As a

16             result, the jurisdictional allocation factors do not recognize that SPS’s proposal to

17             directly assign the costs of the Cunningham BESS solely to New Mexico retail

 2        shared system.

 3   Q.   WHAT IS THE IMPACT OF THIS APPROACH?

 4   A.   Because the Company does not adjust its jurisdictional production allocator to

 5        reflect the direct assignment of the Cunningham BESS, this creates a mismatch

 6        between cost responsibility and system benefits that is inconsistent with cost

 7        causation principles. If New Mexico customers are to pay for and receive the full

 8        benefits of a capacity resource like the Cunningham BESS, their reliance on other

 9        shared system capacity resources is necessarily reduced. Absent an adjustment to

10        the jurisdictional production allocator, New Mexico retail customers are at risk of

11        paying twice for the same capacity through (1) the full cost of the directly assigned

12        Cunningham BESS, and through (2) an unadjusted share of all other system

13        capacity through the 12-CP PROD allocator, which continues to treat New Mexico

14        customers as fully reliant on the shared system despite the direct assignment of the

15        Cunningham BESS. Because SPS proposes to directly assign the capacity from

16        the Cunningham BESS to New Mexico, one would expect New Mexico to need

17        less and Texas to need more of the remaining system capacity resources.

18               Further, the Company’s approach is inconsistent with the Company’s

19        application requesting to allocate to New Mexico 100% of the costs and benefits

 2              receive the full benefit of the resource if they are subject to bear an unadjusted

 3              share of shared system capacity costs in addition to the costs of the directly

 4              assigned resource.

 5                      Finally, in a recent Recommended Decision addressing the proposed direct

 6              allocation of SPS’s Sandy Loam Solar facility, the Hearing Examiner stated that,

 7              “[i]t is not just and reasonable to direct all the costs to New Mexico customers and

 8              then deprive those customers of the credit for the system wide capacity benefit that

 9              that facility is providing.”9

13             Mexico load served by the accredited capacity of the Cunningham BESS from the

14             shared system capacity pool used to allocate shared system production resources.

QUESTION NO. NMLCG 3-39:

     Plant Additions. Please refer to page 32 of Mark Lytal’s direct testimony regarding
     “Gaines County Unit 0 – Interconnection,” which Attachment ML-3 reflects as being
     placed in service in May 2026.

        a. State whether the capital investment of $25,028,433 associated with the Gaines
           County Unit 0 – Interconnection facilities is included in the Company’s CCN
           request in Case No. 25-00066-UT.

        b. Please explain the basis for which the Company assumes the Gaines County Unit 0
           – Interconnection asset(s) are used and useful as of May 2026, including how the
           facility will be serving customer load or benefiting the system.


ORIGINAL RESPONSE:

     SPS has requested an extension to provide this response on March 25.

MARCH 24, 2026, SUPPLEMENTAL RESPONSE:

        a. Yes. The capital investment is included in the network upgrade category of costs
           in Case No. 25-00066-UT.

        b. The capital investment for Gaines County Unit 0 consists of a required payment to
           the Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) under the generator interconnection study
           process—the Definitive Interconnection System Impact Study (DISIS)—to
           maintain SPS’s interconnection rights and queue position for the Gaines County
           gas-fired generation project. Preservation of the DISIS queue position was
           necessary for the project to be bid into SPS’s 2024 Resource Request for Proposals
           and evaluated as part of the 2025 generation portfolio presented for approval in
           Case No. 25-00066-UT.

            The DISIS queue preservation payment is an enabling, process-driven
            interconnection cost required to maintain SPS’s position in the SPP generator
            interconnection study process. This cost is separate and distinct from the ultimate
            approval, construction, or in-servicing of the specific generating facility.

             Maintaining the queue position provides value to customers by preserving SPS’s
             ability to timely pursue least-cost capacity resources needed to serve load and meet
             resource adequacy requirements.

             As reflected in SPS’s accepted 2023 Integrated Resource Plan and the record in
             Case No. 25-00066-UT, SPS faces an immediate need for additional capacity. In
             this context, preserving the DISIS queue position was necessary to keep viable,
             timely, and least-cost capacity options available. The payment was therefore
             prudently incurred based on the information known at the time, consistent with
             SPS’s obligation to plan for reliable and affordable service.

             SPS’s request to include this investment in rate base in this case is appropriate
             because the “Gaines County Unit 0 – Interconnection” is a capitalized pre-
             operational cost that preserves SPS’s capability to meet identified customer needs.
             This payment is not speculative development dependent on a finding that the
             generating unit is used and useful; rather, it is a necessary interconnection-related
             investment incurred to preserve SPS’s ability to meet a demonstrated near-term
             capacity need at least cost. Inclusion of this enabling investment in rate base
             appropriately recognizes that the cost ais reasonable, necessary, and prudent.
